name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: An instructor reviews how a student earns their BLS course completion card. According to AHA Part 1, what minimum passing score is required on the written exam in the instructor-led course?

answers.text: 60 percent
75 percent
84 percent
99 percent

explanations.a: Sixty percent is below the AHA-specified minimum and would not qualify for course completion.
explanations.b: Seventy-five percent is below the BLS minimum specified in the manual.
explanations.c: AHA Part 1 specifies a minimum passing score of 84 percent on the written exam of the instructor-led BLS course.
explanations.d: Ninety-nine percent is far above the AHA-specified minimum; the threshold is 84 percent.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: AHA Part 1 lists the skills tests a student must pass to earn a BLS course completion card. Which two tests are required?

answers.text: The Adult CPR and AED Skills Test and the Infant CPR Skills Test
Only the Adult CPR Skills Test
The Bag-Mask Skills Test and the Stroke Recognition Skills Test
A 5-day clinical rotation in a hospital

explanations.a: AHA Part 1 names the Adult CPR and AED Skills Test and the Infant CPR Skills Test as the two skills tests required to receive the course completion card.
explanations.b: Both adult and infant skills are tested separately to verify across-age-group competence.
explanations.c: Bag-mask skills and stroke recognition are taught and tested as components, not as the named skills tests.
explanations.d: BLS is a course completion card, not a clinical rotation requirement.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: AHA Part 1's high-quality CPR callout sets a target for how quickly compressions must begin once cardiac arrest is recognized. What is that target?

answers.text: Within 30 seconds after recognizing cardiac arrest
Within 10 seconds after recognizing cardiac arrest
Within 1 minute after recognizing cardiac arrest
Within 5 minutes after recognizing cardiac arrest

explanations.a: Thirty seconds is too long; the AHA-specified target is faster.
explanations.b: AHA Part 1 specifies starting compressions within 10 seconds after recognizing cardiac arrest.
explanations.c: A 1-minute delay would significantly reduce coronary perfusion pressure.
explanations.d: Five minutes is far past the AHA threshold and would devastate survival.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: Your CPR feedback monitor shows an average compression depth of 2.6 inches (6.6 cm) on an adult. AHA Part 1 explicitly caps adult depth. What is the upper limit?

answers.text: No more than 1.5 inches (4 cm)
No more than 2 inches (5 cm)
No more than 2.4 inches (6 cm)
No more than 4 inches (10 cm)

explanations.a: 1.5 inches is the infant depth target, not the adult ceiling.
explanations.b: 2 inches is the adult minimum depth, not the upper cap.
explanations.c: AHA Part 1 specifies adult compressions should be at least 2 inches (5 cm) but no more than 2.4 inches (6 cm).
explanations.d: Four inches is dangerously beyond the AHA-specified upper limit.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: AHA Part 1's high-quality CPR callout describes how rescuers should give each rescue breath. Which combination matches?

answers.text: Deliver each breath over 1 second, using only enough volume to make the chest rise; avoid excessive ventilation
Deliver each breath over 5 seconds, with maximum volume
Skip breaths entirely during BLS
Deliver each breath as forcefully as possible to overcome resistance

explanations.a: AHA Part 1 specifies delivering each breath over 1 second, using only enough volume to make the person's chest rise, and avoiding excessive ventilation.
explanations.b: Five-second maximum-volume breaths cause hyperinflation and gastric inflation.
explanations.c: BLS providers are expected to give breaths, not skip them; only untrained lay rescuers default to compressions only.
explanations.d: Forceful breaths cause gastric inflation and may reduce cardiac output.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: A BLS student asks what counts as PPE for an emergency response. Which set of items best matches the AHA Part 1 description?

answers.text: Only sterile gloves on the dominant hand
A combination of items such as medical gloves, eye protection, gowns, high-visibility clothing, safety footwear, and helmets
A defibrillator and naloxone kit
A face shield only, used as a single-rescuer mouthpiece

explanations.a: PPE is more comprehensive than a single sterile glove and is not limited to the dominant hand.
explanations.b: AHA Part 1 says PPE varies by situation and may include medical gloves, eye protection, gowns or full-body suits, high-visibility clothing, safety footwear, and helmets.
explanations.c: AEDs and medications are emergency response equipment that treat the patient, not PPE that protects the rescuer.
explanations.d: A face shield alone is one barrier device; PPE is broader and varies by situation.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: A new BLS provider asks who decides which PPE they must wear in the workplace. According to AHA Part 1, where should they look for the role-specific PPE protocols?

answers.text: Only the BLS Provider Manual lists every required item
A nationally posted list with no local variation
Their employer, local health authority, or regulatory body
The patient or family at the scene

explanations.a: The BLS manual gives general categories and defers to local authorities for role-specific requirements.
explanations.b: PPE requirements vary by setting and jurisdiction; no single national list overrides local rules.
explanations.c: AHA Part 1 directs rescuers to ask their employer, local health authority, or regulatory body about PPE protocols for their role.
explanations.d: Patients and families do not set rescuer PPE protocols and may not know what is required.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: AHA Part 1 defines an 'infant' for BLS purposes. Which range matches the manual's definition?

answers.text: From age 1 through puberty
Younger than 1 year, excluding newly born infants in the delivery room
From birth through age 5
Younger than 6 months only

explanations.a: From 1 year to puberty defines a child, not an infant.
explanations.b: AHA Part 1 defines an infant as someone younger than 1 year, excluding newly born infants in the delivery room.
explanations.c: Birth through age 5 spans both infant and child categories.
explanations.d: The infant category extends through the first year of life, not just the first 6 months.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: You are caring for a 13-year-old who has visible chest hair and is in cardiac arrest. According to AHA Part 1, which BLS approach is appropriate?

answers.text: Use pediatric BLS based on chronologic age
Use neonatal resuscitation guidelines
Wait for parental consent before any care
Treat as an adult because there are signs of puberty

explanations.a: AHA defines the adult range as starting at puberty, regardless of chronologic age below 18.
explanations.b: Neonatal guidelines apply to the newly born in the delivery room, not adolescents.
explanations.c: Cardiac arrest care is provided under implied consent; waiting for parental consent delays critical treatment.
explanations.d: AHA Part 1 lists chest or underarm hair on males and any breast development on females as signs of puberty, after which BLS treats the patient as an adult.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: Which range does AHA Part 1 use to define a 'child' for BLS purposes?

answers.text: From 1 year of age to puberty
From birth to age 2
From age 6 to age 12 only
Anyone younger than 18 regardless of physical development

explanations.a: AHA Part 1 defines a child as anyone from 1 year of age to the onset of puberty.
explanations.b: Birth-to-2 includes infants and only the youngest children, not the full child range.
explanations.c: Restricting to ages 6-12 excludes younger children in the BLS pediatric range.
explanations.d: Adolescents who have reached puberty are treated as adults under BLS, not as children.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.objective: 1.5 Chain of Survival overview and prevention
questions.text: AHA Part 2 describes one element that underlies the entire Chain of Survival rather than appearing as a single link. Which element does it describe in this way?

answers.text: Cardiac catheterization availability
Public access defibrillation
Rapid response team activation
Prevention of cardiac arrest

explanations.a: Cardiac catheterization is part of post-cardiac arrest care, not the foundation underlying every link.
explanations.b: Public access defibrillation supports the defibrillation link specifically rather than serving as the foundation of the chain.
explanations.c: Rapid response teams are an in-hospital tactic, not the foundation of the entire chain.
explanations.d: Per AHA Part 2, prevention of cardiac arrest is the foundation of the Chain of Survival, supported by public awareness, training, and emergency response system development.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.objective: 1.5 Chain of Survival overview and prevention
questions.keyword: double or triple survival CPR defib
questions.text: A coworker asks why bystander CPR matters when EMS will arrive in a few minutes. Which statement best summarizes the AHA Part 2 conclusion about combining high-quality CPR with early defibrillation?

answers.text: It can double or triple the chances of survival
It improves survival by less than five percent in any setting
It only matters when the arrest happens inside a hospital
It has no effect until ALS arrives

explanations.a: AHA Part 2 states that high-quality CPR started immediately combined with early defibrillation can double or triple the chances of survival.
explanations.b: Survival improvement is far greater than five percent — bystander CPR with defibrillation can multiply survival several-fold.
explanations.c: The benefit applies in both in-hospital and out-of-hospital settings.
explanations.d: CPR and defibrillation are the foundation of survival; waiting for ALS without them dramatically lowers survival.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.objective: 1.6 The six Chain of Survival links
questions.text: An instructor draws the AHA Chain of Survival on the board and asks students to identify the very first link a rescuer acts on when someone collapses. Which link is it?

answers.text: Defibrillation
Recognition and emergency activation
Advanced resuscitation
Post-cardiac arrest care

explanations.a: Defibrillation is the third link, applied after recognition has triggered EMS activation and CPR has begun.
explanations.b: Recognition and emergency activation is the first link — the rescuer recognizes the arrest and activates the emergency response system.
explanations.c: Advanced resuscitation occurs once a high-performance team has taken over, well after the first link.
explanations.d: Post-cardiac arrest care follows return of spontaneous circulation, near the end of the chain rather than the beginning.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.objective: 1.6 The six Chain of Survival links
questions.text: You are reviewing the six AHA Chain of Survival links to teach a community CPR class. Which sequence places the links in the correct order from first to last?

answers.text: High-quality CPR, recognition, defibrillation, advanced resuscitation, recovery, post-arrest care
Defibrillation, recognition, CPR, recovery, advanced resuscitation, post-arrest care
Recognition, defibrillation, CPR, post-arrest care, advanced resuscitation, recovery
Recognition and activation, high-quality CPR, defibrillation, advanced resuscitation, post-cardiac arrest care, recovery and survivorship

explanations.a: High-quality CPR cannot precede recognition — you have to know an arrest is happening before compressions begin.
explanations.b: Defibrillation cannot precede recognition; rhythm cannot be analyzed before the AED is even called for.
explanations.c: Post-arrest care must follow advanced resuscitation, not precede it, because it begins after return of spontaneous circulation.
explanations.d: The AHA chain runs recognition and activation, high-quality CPR, defibrillation, advanced resuscitation, post-cardiac arrest care, then recovery and survivorship.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: A hospital quality committee compares how the Chain of Survival is applied inside the hospital versus on the street. Which characteristic distinguishes the in-hospital approach according to AHA Part 2?

answers.text: It relies primarily on lay rescuers locating a public AED
It avoids advanced interventions to keep care simple
It does not include defibrillation as a link
It focuses on prevention and early recognition through monitoring, with rapid response or medical emergency teams

explanations.a: Lay rescuer and public AED dependence describes the out-of-hospital setting, not in-hospital care.
explanations.b: Hospitals are where advanced interventions like vascular access, medications, and advanced airways are most readily available.
explanations.c: Defibrillation remains a core link in both settings; the hospital simply uses monitor/defibrillators in addition to AEDs.
explanations.d: AHA Part 2 says in-hospital care emphasizes prevention and early recognition with monitoring, supported by rapid response or medical emergency teams.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.keyword: OHCA depends on lay rescuers EMS
questions.text: AHA Part 2 Table 1 contrasts initial support for in-hospital and out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. Which description matches the out-of-hospital column?

answers.text: Depends on community and EMS professionals for support
Depends on the cardiac catheterization lab being available
Depends on a multidisciplinary team in an intensive care unit
Depends on a pre-existing rapid response team

explanations.a: AHA Part 2 Table 1 says out-of-hospital cardiac arrest depends on community and EMS professionals for initial support.
explanations.b: The cath lab is part of post-arrest care, not initial out-of-hospital support.
explanations.c: ICU teams operate inside the hospital and are not the source of initial OHCA support.
explanations.d: Rapid response teams are an in-hospital structure, not an out-of-hospital one.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: After a long, unsuccessful resuscitation attempt, a team leader reviews AHA recovery and survivorship guidance with the rescuers. Which statement most accurately reflects that guidance?

answers.text: Recovery support is only relevant for the patient, never for rescuers
Cardiac rehabilitation should be skipped to reduce health care costs
Rescuers and caregivers may benefit from psychological support, resiliency, burnout prevention, and effective debriefing after the event
Family members of survivors should not be involved in recovery

explanations.a: AHA Part 2 extends recovery and survivorship considerations beyond the patient to caregivers and rescuers.
explanations.b: Cardiac rehabilitation is a specific recommended intervention for many survivors and is not framed as optional based on cost.
explanations.c: AHA Part 2 explicitly says rescuers and caregivers may benefit from psychological support, resiliency, burnout prevention, and effective debriefing.
explanations.d: Family members are part of the support network and AHA encourages a multimodal recovery approach.

questions.name: Course Concepts and Chain of Survival
questions.text: An untrained bystander calls 911 after a stranger collapses. The emergency telecommunicator coaches the caller through chest compressions until EMS arrives. AHA Part 2 identifies this practice by which abbreviation?

answers.text: PAD
PALS
ROSC
T-CPR

explanations.a: PAD stands for public access defibrillation — about device placement, not phone-coached compressions.
explanations.b: PALS is pediatric advanced life support, an in-person clinical intervention rather than dispatcher coaching.
explanations.c: ROSC is return of spontaneous circulation, a clinical state rather than a coaching practice.
explanations.d: T-CPR is telecommunicator-assisted CPR, the dispatcher-guided coaching that helps untrained callers perform high-quality compressions.
